Editor's note: Campbell Brown anchors CNN's "Campbell Brown: No Bias, No Bull" at 8 p.m. ET Mondays through Fridays. She delivered this commentary during the "Cutting through the Bull" segment of Monday night's broadcast. CNN's Campbell Brown says nonemergency legislation needs time to be read by the public and Congress. (CNN) -- Whether by omission or commission, both the White House and Congress get a dose of blame for not living up to the new era of transparency promised by President Obama. The president's old campaign Web site still has this commitment there for all to see: . "As president, Obama will not sign any nonemergency bill without giving the American public an opportunity to review and comment on the White House Web site for five days." Well, the president broke that promise barely a week after taking office when he signed the Lilly Ledbetter Bill dealing with equal pay for men and women. A good bill, and certainly one that could have survived a five-day comment period. So, maybe the White House folks just forgot? But then there is Congress and the Stimulus Bill. How fast could you get through it? According to the nonpartisan Sunlight Foundation, lawmakers had just 13 hours to read 1,100 pages of material that would cost the American taxpayer $787 billion. That's less than a minute and a half per page, with no time for bathroom breaks. No wonder so many of our lawmakers didn't seem to notice that last-minute exemption clearing the way for bailed-out companies like AIG to pay out big bonuses. So, the House tried to clean up the mess last week by rushing through another bill -- a tax on AIG bonuses. That bill was just 11 hours old before it went on the floor to be argued and then quickly approved. And the list goes on well before the president took office. The bank bailout got all of 29 hours, the rescue of Fannie and Freddie was only available for 19 hours. This is how bills could literally become, to borrow a phrase, too big to fail -- and too fast to stop. The Sunlight Foundation is calling on Congress to allow the American people three days, 72 hours, to read a nonemergency bill online before debate begins. We strongly agree. And yes lawmakers, you can have three days to read it over, too, before taking a stand. As for President Obama's promise of a five-day public review once a bill leaves Capitol Hill headed for his desk, it would be nice if he kept his word on this going forward. The opinions expressed in this commentary are solely those of Campbell Brown.

**Editor’s Note:** Campbell Brown anchors CNN’s *Campbell Brown: No Bias, No Bull* at 8 p.m. ET, Monday through Friday. She delivered this commentary during the “Cutting through the Bull” segment of Monday night’s broadcast.

CNN’s Campbell Brown says nonemergency legislation needs time to be read by both the public and Congress.

**(CNN) --** Whether by omission or commission, both the White House and Congress deserve a measure of blame for failing to live up to the new era of transparency promised by President Obama.

The president’s former campaign website still displays this commitment for all to see: “As president, Obama will not sign any nonemergency bill without giving the American public an opportunity to review and comment on the White House website for five days.”

Yet the president broke that promise barely a week after taking office, when he signed the Lilly Ledbetter Bill, which addressed equal pay for men and women. It was a good bill—and certainly one that could have withstood a five-day public comment period. So perhaps White House staff simply forgot?

But then there is Congress and the Stimulus Bill. How quickly could anyone reasonably get through it? According to the nonpartisan Sunlight Foundation, lawmakers had just 13 hours to read 1,100 pages of material that would cost American taxpayers $787 billion. That is less than a minute and a half per page, with no time for bathroom breaks.

No wonder so many lawmakers seemed not to notice the last-minute exemption that cleared the way for bailed-out companies such as AIG to pay large bonuses.

So, the House attempted to clean up the mess last week by rushing through another bill—a tax on AIG bonuses. That bill was only 11 hours old before it reached the floor for debate and was then swiftly approved.

And the list extends well back before the president took office. The bank bailout received all of 29 hours for review; the rescue of Fannie and Freddie was available for only 19 hours.

This is how bills can quite literally become, to borrow a phrase, too big to fail—and too fast to stop.

The Sunlight Foundation is calling on Congress to allow the American people three days—72 hours—to read any nonemergency bill online before debate begins. We strongly agree. And yes, lawmakers, you may have three days to read it over as well before taking a stand.

As for President Obama’s promise of a five-day public review once a bill leaves Capitol Hill and heads to his desk, it would be encouraging to see him keep his word on this going forward.

The opinions expressed in this commentary are solely those of Campbell Brown.

Editor’s note: Campbell Brown hosts CNN’s *Campbell Brown: No Bias, No Bull* weeknights at 8 p.m. ET. She gave this commentary during Monday night’s “Cutting through the Bull” segment. CNN’s Campbell Brown argues that nonemergency bills should be given enough time for both the public and members of Congress to read them.

(CNN) — Through action or inaction, the White House and Congress both deserve criticism for falling short of the level of openness President Obama pledged to bring to government.

That promise is still visible on the president’s former campaign website: “As president, Obama will not sign any nonemergency bill without giving the American public an opportunity to review and comment on the White House Web site for five days.”

Yet just over a week into his presidency, Obama failed to honor that pledge when he signed the Lilly Ledbetter Bill, which addressed equal pay for women and men. It was worthwhile legislation, and it surely could have withstood five days of public review and feedback.

So perhaps the White House simply overlooked the commitment.

But Congress has its own example: the Stimulus Bill. How quickly could anyone reasonably read it? The nonpartisan Sunlight Foundation reported that legislators were given only 13 hours to go through 1,100 pages of material involving $787 billion in taxpayer money. That works out to under 90 seconds per page, with no time even for a restroom break.

Given that, it is hardly surprising that many lawmakers appeared to miss a late-added provision that allowed rescued companies such as AIG to hand out large bonuses.

Then, last week, the House attempted to fix the problem by hurrying through yet another piece of legislation — a tax on AIG bonuses. That bill had existed for only 11 hours before it was brought to the floor for debate and swiftly passed.

And the pattern predates Obama’s presidency. The bank bailout was available for only 29 hours, while the rescue package for Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac could be reviewed for just 19 hours.

This is how legislation can become, to use a familiar phrase, too large to fail — and move too quickly to be stopped.

The Sunlight Foundation is urging Congress to give Americans three days — 72 hours — to examine any nonemergency bill online before debate starts. We fully support that idea.

And lawmakers, yes, you should get those same three days to read the legislation before deciding where you stand.

As for President Obama’s pledge to provide five days of public review after a bill has passed Congress and is on its way to his desk, it would be good to see him honor that promise from now on.

The views stated in this commentary belong only to Campbell Brown.

Campbell Brown argues that both the White House and Congress have fallen short of their promises to make government more transparent and accountable. During the campaign and after taking office, President Obama spoke often about changing the way Washington works, including a pledge that major legislation would be posted publicly before it was signed so citizens could read it and lawmakers could be held responsible for what they approved. Brown contends that this principle should not be treated as a campaign slogan or a symbolic gesture, but as a basic requirement of responsible governing.

Her central point is simple: unless a bill is responding to a true emergency, the public and members of Congress should have enough time to examine it before it becomes law. Legislation often runs hundreds or even thousands of pages, with complex provisions, spending commitments, tax changes, and regulatory language that can have enormous consequences. When lawmakers are asked to vote on such bills with little time to read or understand them, mistakes become more likely, special-interest provisions can slip through unnoticed, and the public is left out of the democratic process.

Brown points to several rushed pieces of legislation as examples of why transparency matters. The economic stimulus package, passed during a moment of financial crisis, was so large and moved so quickly that many lawmakers had little opportunity to study all of its details before voting. While supporters argued that speed was necessary to respond to the recession, Brown suggests that urgency should not excuse abandoning scrutiny altogether. A bill involving hundreds of billions of taxpayer dollars deserved careful review, not just rapid approval.

She also highlights the controversy over bonuses paid to executives at AIG after the company received federal bailout money. Public outrage led Congress to move quickly on a punitive tax bill aimed at reclaiming those bonuses. But Brown argues that this response was another example of legislating in haste. In the rush to appear tough and responsive, lawmakers risked creating poorly considered policy, raising constitutional and practical questions that might have been identified earlier through a more deliberate review process.

For Brown, these incidents demonstrate a broader problem in Washington: leaders often defend speed as necessary, especially during crises, but speed can also become an excuse for carelessness. When legislation is pushed through before citizens, journalists, watchdog groups, and even legislators themselves have time to examine it, the chances of waste, loopholes, unintended consequences, and political grandstanding increase dramatically.

She is not arguing that government should be paralyzed or that every bill must be delayed indefinitely. Genuine emergencies may require swift action. But for ordinary, nonemergency legislation, Brown insists that transparency should be nonnegotiable. Bills should be made publicly available for a meaningful period before votes are taken or before the president signs them into law. That waiting period would allow experts to analyze the language, citizens to contact their representatives, and lawmakers to understand what they are approving.

Ultimately, Brown’s criticism is about trust. If elected officials promise openness but continue to pass major legislation behind closed doors or under extreme time pressure, they deepen public cynicism about government. Transparency is not merely a procedural nicety; it is a safeguard against flawed governance. By allowing time for review, debate, and public input, Washington can reduce costly mistakes and better honor the democratic principles it claims to defend.

---

## Commentary: Public Deserves Time to Read Nonemergency Bills Before Congress Votes

When Congress rushes major legislation to the floor, lawmakers often defend the pace by saying the situation demands urgency. Sometimes, that is true. In a genuine emergency — a natural disaster, a financial panic, a national security crisis — speed can matter.

But not every bill is an emergency. And when legislation is not urgent, the public deserves time to see what is in it before elected officials vote.

That was the core criticism aimed at President Obama and Congress during debates over transparency and legislative process: promises of openness sounded good on the campaign trail, but in practice, major bills were still being pushed forward with little time for public review.

The issue is not just procedural. It goes to trust.

If a bill affects taxes, spending, health care, energy policy, or regulation, Americans should have a reasonable opportunity to read it — or at least for journalists, watchdog groups, advocacy organizations, and ordinary citizens to examine it — before it becomes law. Posting legislation online for several days before a vote is not a radical demand. It is basic accountability.

Lawmakers frequently complain that the public does not understand what Congress is doing. But the public cannot understand what it is not allowed to see in time.

The same standard should apply no matter which party is in power. Republicans criticized Democrats for rushing bills. Democrats criticized Republicans for doing the same. Both parties have used urgency, complexity, and backroom negotiations to justify moving legislation before scrutiny catches up.

That is exactly why the rule should not depend on political convenience.

For nonemergency bills, Congress should provide a clear public review period before final passage. If leaders believe a bill is strong, they should not fear sunlight. If they believe the policy is defensible, they should be willing to let the country inspect it.

Transparency does not guarantee good legislation. But secrecy and speed almost always make bad legislation easier to pass.

The public’s business should be done in public — and with enough time for the public to actually know what is being done.

counterfactuals.output:
## Editor’s Note

Transparency in government is not a partisan luxury; it is a democratic necessity. During the 2008 campaign, Barack Obama promised that, as president, he would allow the public five days to review non-emergency legislation before signing it. But the early rush surrounding major legislation — including the economic stimulus package — raised legitimate questions about whether that promise would be honored in practice.

The controversy over bonuses paid to executives at AIG, after the company received massive taxpayer support, only sharpened public concern about what lawmakers knew, when they knew it, and whether major provisions in complex bills were being scrutinized before becoming law.

In the commentary below, Campbell Brown argues that Congress and the White House should embrace a simple rule championed by transparency advocates such as the Sunlight Foundation: post major legislation online for at least 72 hours before a vote, giving lawmakers, journalists, watchdog groups, and citizens time to read the fine print.

---

## Opinion Commentary  
### Transparency Should Not Be Optional in Washington  
*By Campbell Brown*

President Obama made a straightforward promise during the campaign: before signing non-emergency legislation, he would give the American people five days to review it online.

It was a good promise. It was also an important one.

After all, if there is one thing voters across the political spectrum agree on, it is that Washington too often does business in the dark. Bills are negotiated behind closed doors. Major provisions appear at the last minute. Lawmakers vote on hundreds — sometimes thousands — of pages they have barely had time to read. Then, when something goes wrong, everyone acts shocked.

We saw this problem play out with the stimulus bill.

The country was in crisis. The economy was shedding jobs. Credit markets were frozen. There was real urgency. But urgency cannot become an excuse for opacity. The American Recovery and Reinvestment Act was one of the largest spending bills in American history, and the public deserved meaningful time to review what was in it before it became law.

Then came the outrage over AIG bonuses.

Taxpayers had poured billions into rescuing the insurance giant, only to learn that executives were receiving large bonuses. Members of Congress rushed to condemn the payments. The administration expressed anger. But the episode raised an obvious question: How did this happen? Were lawmakers fully aware of the language affecting those bonuses? Did anyone have enough time to examine the details before voting?

That is exactly why transparency matters.

It is not just about symbolism. It is not just about posting documents online and checking a box. Transparency is a safeguard against bad lawmaking. It gives watchdogs time to catch problems. It gives journalists time to ask questions. It gives lawmakers time to understand what they are actually voting on. Most importantly, it gives citizens a chance to see what is being done in their name and with their money.

The Sunlight Foundation has proposed a simple reform: require that legislation be posted online for at least 72 hours before Congress votes on it.

That should not be controversial.

Seventy-two hours is not an eternity. It is three days. If a bill is truly an emergency, there can be a narrow exception. But most legislation — especially major spending bills — should be available for public review before lawmakers cast their votes. Not after. Not when it is too late to matter.

Some in Washington will say this slows down the process. Good. Sometimes the process needs to slow down.

When Congress is spending hundreds of billions of dollars, rewriting major policy, or inserting provisions that affect private contracts and taxpayer obligations, a pause is not a problem. It is a responsibility.

President Obama was right when he said the public should have time to review legislation. Now the White House and Congress should live by that principle. The five-day promise should be honored whenever possible. At the very least, the 72-hour rule should become standard practice.

This is not about Republicans versus Democrats. Both parties have abused the legislative process when it suited them. Both parties have rushed bills through Congress. Both parties have hidden behind complexity and urgency.

And both parties should be held to the same standard.

If lawmakers believe in a bill, they should not be afraid to let the public read it. If the White House supports legislation, it should welcome scrutiny before the president signs it. If there is nothing to hide, then prove it.

Washington keeps asking Americans to trust it. But trust is earned. And it starts with letting the public see the fine print before the deal is done.

Tonight, a simple question: What is the rush?

Again and again, major pieces of legislation — bills that could reshape the economy, health care, national security, taxation, or the lives of millions of Americans — are being pushed through Congress at breakneck speed. Hundreds, sometimes thousands, of pages appear just hours before a vote. Lawmakers are expected to make decisions of enormous consequence before they, their staffs, the press, or the public have had a meaningful chance to read what is actually in the bill.

That should trouble everyone, regardless of party.

This is not a Democratic problem or a Republican problem. Both parties have done it when they had the votes and the clock was working in their favor. Leaders argue that deadlines are urgent, that negotiations have dragged on long enough, that compromise requires moving quickly before support collapses. Sometimes those arguments may be politically convenient. Occasionally, they may even be true.

But democracy is not supposed to operate on a “trust us” basis.

If a bill is important enough to affect every household in America, it is important enough to be read. If lawmakers are going to spend hundreds of billions — or trillions — of taxpayer dollars, they should be able to explain what they are voting for. And if the public is expected to live with the consequences, then the public deserves time to understand them.

Too often, we hear members of Congress complain after the fact that they did not know a provision was included, or that language had been changed at the last minute, or that the real impact only became clear once agencies began implementing the law. That is not a minor procedural flaw. That is a failure of basic responsibility.

The answer is not complicated: post the full text of major bills well before a vote. Give lawmakers time to read them. Give journalists time to scrutinize them. Give citizens time to call their representatives and weigh in. Emergency legislation may sometimes require speed, but “emergency” cannot become the permanent excuse for avoiding transparency.

Congress was not elected merely to vote. It was elected to deliberate.

And when legislation is rushed through before anyone can fully understand it, the message to the public is unmistakable: the details are for insiders, and the consequences are for everyone else.

That is not how accountable government is supposed to work.

**Opinion: No bill should become law before the public can read it**

*Editor’s note: The following is an original opinion-style piece inspired by the public-accountability theme associated with “Campbell Brown: No Bias, No Bull.”*

Washington has a transparency problem — and it is not a partisan one.

Too often, members of Congress are asked to vote on major legislation they have barely had time to read. Too often, the public learns what is in a bill only after it has passed. And too often, the president is handed legislation for signature before Americans have had a meaningful chance to understand what their government is about to do in their name.

That should end.

Congress and the White House should adopt a simple rule: For all nonemergency legislation, the final text of a bill should be posted online for a reasonable period of time before Congress votes on it and before the president signs it.

This is not a radical idea. It is basic democratic hygiene.

If a bill is important enough to become law, it is important enough for the public to read. If lawmakers believe legislation deserves support, they should be willing to defend the actual text — not a summary, not talking points, not a press release, but the bill itself.

The public should not have to rely on leaks, lobbyists or last-minute spin to understand what Congress is doing. Posting legislation online would allow journalists, watchdog groups, experts, businesses, local officials and ordinary citizens to examine the details before they become binding law.

The details matter. A single paragraph can create a loophole. A tucked-away provision can benefit a narrow interest. A few words can change how billions of dollars are spent. When legislation is rushed through in the dark, the people with the most access — lobbyists, insiders and political operatives — are often the only ones who know what is really happening.

Transparency will not solve every problem in Washington. It will not guarantee good policy. It will not end partisanship. But it would make it harder to hide bad policy.

There should, of course, be an exception for genuine emergencies. If the nation is responding to an attack, a natural disaster, a financial panic or another urgent crisis, government must be able to act quickly. But “emergency” should not become a magic word used to avoid scrutiny. The exception should be narrow, public and justified in writing.

For ordinary legislation, a waiting period is reasonable. Posting bills online for at least 72 hours before a vote would give Americans time to review the text. Posting the final legislation again before presidential signature would ensure that the version approved by Congress is the version the public sees before it becomes law.

Some lawmakers may object that Congress already moves too slowly. But transparency is not the reason Washington is dysfunctional. Backroom bargaining, political gamesmanship and sprawling bills negotiated behind closed doors are part of the problem. A public posting requirement would encourage lawmakers to write clearer bills and think twice before adding controversial provisions at the last minute.

Others may say ordinary Americans do not read legislative text. Maybe not always. But that misses the point. The public has a right to access it. Reporters can read it. Legal experts can read it. Advocacy groups across the political spectrum can read it. Citizens who care deeply about a particular issue can read it. Democracy depends not on every person reading every page, but on the ability of anyone to inspect what government is doing.

This should not be a Democratic idea or a Republican idea. Both parties have criticized secrecy when they are out of power and embraced speed when they are in power. That hypocrisy is exactly why the rule should be institutional, not optional.

Presidents, too, should be held to the same standard. Candidates often promise openness. Once in office, the pressure to move quickly can take over. A president who receives nonemergency legislation should commit not to sign it until the final text has been publicly available online for a set period of time.

This is about trust. Americans are deeply skeptical of Washington, and not without reason. They see enormous bills passed under deadline pressure. They hear elected officials admit they have not read everything they voted on. They watch special provisions surface only after the fact. Then they are told to trust the process.

Trust has to be earned.

Posting legislation online before votes and signatures would be a small but meaningful step toward earning it. It would tell the public: We are not afraid for you to see what we are doing. It would tell lawmakers: You are accountable for the words on the page. And it would tell lobbyists and insiders: The public gets a look, too.

No bias. No bull. Just put the bills online before they become law.
